vignette:
The Weight of What Was Done

Raymond is a 72-year-old software engineer who still works part-time as a consultant, writing code from the spare bedroom of his small apartment in Vancouver. He has never married. He keeps his schedule precise and his world deliberately small, and for decades he has told himself this is simply who he is - a man who prefers order and solitude. It has taken him a long time to consider that these preferences might not be preferences at all.

In 1978, Raymond was twenty-eight years old and working as a telecommunications engineer on contract in a Central American country whose political situation he had understood only vaguely before he arrived. He was detained by government security forces during a sweep of a neighborhood where he happened to be visiting a colleague. What followed lasted eleven days. He does not speak about the specifics easily, and when he does, he does so in a flat, almost technical register - the same voice he uses to describe a debugging problem. He was beaten. He was subjected to stress positions and sleep deprivation. At one point, he believed with complete certainty that he would not leave that building alive. He did leave. He has never been entirely sure why.

He returned to Canada, told his family he had been briefly detained on a misunderstanding, and went back to work within three weeks. This was, he explains, simply what one did. He was from a generation and a family culture in which the correct response to suffering was to continue. And for a long time, continuation looked like success. He built a career. He was good at his work - still is. The logic of code suited him. It was honest. It did what it was told.

But the nights were never right. For years he drank moderately to help himself sleep, then less moderately, then he stopped drinking altogether in his late forties after a period he describes only as "a bad stretch." Even now, sleep is something he negotiates rather than enjoys. He wakes at irregular hours with his heart already loud in his chest, the details of the room needing a moment to reassemble themselves into safety. Sometimes there is no clear image attached to the waking - just a physical certainty of threat, as though his body received a message his conscious mind did not.

Certain things still move through him without warning. The sound of a door being locked from the outside. Fluorescent lighting in a particular frequency. The smell of a specific industrial cleaning product he has encountered twice in hospital waiting rooms, both times requiring him to leave immediately and stand outside in the cold until his hands stopped shaking. He finds these reactions embarrassing and has, until recently, worked around them quietly and alone.

What brought Raymond to therapy was not a crisis but an accumulation. His consulting work has moved increasingly to video calls, and he finds himself hypervigilant during meetings in ways that exhaust him - scanning faces, reading silences, bracing for something he cannot name. He has begun avoiding calls altogether when he can, submitting work asynchronously, retreating further. He notices he has fewer and fewer reasons to leave the apartment. He does not describe himself as depressed, exactly. He describes himself as tired in a way that sleep does not fix.

Raymond speaks about the past with the careful precision of someone who has spent decades organizing it into a manageable shape. He is intelligent and self-aware, and he knows, intellectually, that what happened to him was serious. What he is only beginning to allow himself to feel is that it was serious to him - that the young man in that room in 1978 was himself, and that the man sitting in the consulting chair now has been carrying him, quietly and without acknowledgment, for forty-four years.
